title: SMR Training
subtitle: Sensorimotor-rhythm training near central cortex
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating smr training within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain smr training without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in smr training.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to smr training.

sections.explainSimply: SMR commonly refers to approximately 12–15 Hz activity over sensorimotor regions during quiet immobility.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Historically linked with motor inhibition and sleep-related outcomes, SMR training has been used in epilepsy, ADHD and insomnia research.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Evidence differs by population and study quality. Central-site EMG, movement suppression and nonspecific training effects require consideration.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Choosing a camera lens: every method emphasises some information and introduces its own distortions.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand smr training to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Stillness may improve the metric without proving the intended cortical mechanism.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using smr training predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Stillness may improve the metric without proving the intended cortical mechanism. Evidence classification: promising in selected contexts; mixed clinical evidence.
